headline: Anthropic Cuts 80% of Claude Code Prompt
summary: Anthropic removed 80% of Claude Code's system prompt, shifting responsibility to developers for providing explicit context. This changes how the AI pair programmer behaves and requires updates to prompt templates and workflows.

slides.title: Claude Code's System Prompt Cut by 80%
slides.subtitle: What changed and why your templates may break
slides.body: Anthropic removed most of Claude Code's built-in instructions. How does this affect your AI coding workflow?
slides.deep_dive: Anthropic's Claude Code previously shipped with a massive system prompt that guided its behavior as an AI pair programmer. In a recent update, they stripped away roughly 80% of that prompt, leaving a leaner core. This means the model now relies more heavily on user-provided context and less on baked-in heuristics. Developers who built custom prompt templates around the old system prompt may see degraded performance unless they adapt.
slides.key_fact: 80% of the system prompt was deleted in the latest update.
slides.why_it_matters: Your existing prompt templates and workflow assumptions may no longer hold; you must adjust how you instruct Claude Code.

slides.title: Claude Code: Local AI Pair Programmer
slides.subtitle: Runs in your IDE, indexes code, proposes diffs
slides.body: Claude Code operates locally, understands your codebase, and suggests changes via structured diffs.
slides.deep_dive: Claude Code is an AI coding assistant that runs as a local agent within your development environment. It builds an abstract syntax tree (AST) index of your project, enabling deep codebase awareness. When you ask it to implement a feature or fix a bug, it reasons over the indexed code and outputs a structured diff that you can apply directly. This local-first design keeps your code private and reduces latency.
slides.key_fact: Local agent with full codebase indexing via AST.
slides.why_it_matters: Enables context-aware AI assistance without sending code to the cloud.
before_items: Large prompt with many built-in behaviors
Implicit test generation and style enforcement
after_items: No default behaviors; all must be specified

slides.title: From Query to Diff: The Execution Flow
slides.subtitle: Four stages transform your request into code changes
slides.body: User query → AST indexing → LLM reasoning → structured diff output.
slides.deep_dive: The process starts when a developer submits a natural language query. The local agent first updates or queries the AST index to gather relevant code context. Then it constructs a prompt combining the reduced system prompt, the user query, and the retrieved context. The LLM (Claude) reasons over this and produces a structured diff artifact. Finally, the agent presents the diff for review and application.
slides.key_fact: Reduced system prompt shifts burden to user-provided context.
slides.why_it_matters: Understanding this flow helps you craft queries that yield better diffs.

slides.title: Claude Code Architecture Overview
slides.subtitle: Editor ↔ Local Agent ↔ Code Index ↔ LLM
slides.body: Four components interact locally for privacy and speed.
slides.deep_dive: The architecture centers on a local agent that mediates between your editor, a code index (AST-based), and the LLM. The editor sends queries and receives diffs. The agent manages the code index, which is incrementally updated as you edit. The LLM runs locally or via a local server, ensuring code never leaves your machine. This design prioritizes data privacy and low latency.
slides.key_fact: All components run locally; no code leaves your machine.
slides.why_it_matters: Local execution enables use in air-gapped or sensitive environments.

slides.title: Input-Output Mechanics
slides.subtitle: Natural language in, structured diff out
slides.body: Input: developer query. Processing: AST index + LLM. Output: reviewable diff.
slides.deep_dive: The developer provides a natural language request (e.g., 'Add error handling to the login function'). The agent retrieves relevant code snippets from the AST index, combines them with the reduced system prompt and the query, and feeds this to the LLM. The LLM outputs a structured diff in a standardized format (e.g., unified diff). The agent then presents this diff in the editor for acceptance or modification.
slides.key_fact: Output is a structured diff, not raw code, enabling safe review.
slides.why_it_matters: Structured diffs integrate cleanly with version control and code review.
slides.input: Natural language query + optional project prompt file
slides.processing: AST index retrieval → prompt assembly → LLM inference
slides.output: Unified diff artifact with file paths and changes

slides.title: Common Pitfalls After Prompt Reduction
slides.subtitle: Less built-in guidance means you must be more explicit
slides.body: Mistake: vague prompts. Fix: provide concrete context and examples.
slides.deep_dive: With 80% of the system prompt gone, Claude Code loses many default behaviors like automatic test generation, style enforcement, and architectural patterns. Developers who previously relied on these implicit behaviors now see incomplete or generic outputs. The solution is to externalize those expectations: include style guides, testing requirements, and architectural constraints directly in your queries or in a project-specific prompt file.
slides.key_fact: Implicit behaviors (tests, style, patterns) are no longer automatic.
slides.why_it_matters: You must now explicitly specify requirements that were previously baked in.
items: Mistake: Assuming Claude writes tests automatically → Fix: Add 'write unit tests' to every query
Mistake: Expecting consistent code style → Fix: Provide a style guide in project prompt
Mistake: Relying on architectural patterns → Fix: Explicitly state pattern (e.g., 'use repository pattern')
Mistake: Using old prompt templates unchanged → Fix: Audit and remove references to deleted system prompt sections

slides.title: Adapt Your Workflow in Three Steps
slides.subtitle: Update templates, test, and iterate
slides.body: 1. Audit templates. 2. Add explicit context. 3. Validate outputs.
slides.deep_dive: Start by reviewing your existing prompt templates and identifying sections that relied on the old system prompt. Replace implicit assumptions with explicit instructions. Then run a suite of typical tasks (refactoring, feature addition, bug fix) and compare outputs. Iterate your templates until the diffs meet your standards. Consider maintaining a project-level prompt file that the agent loads automatically.
slides.key_fact: Explicit context replaces the deleted 80% system prompt.
slides.why_it_matters: Proactive adaptation restores productivity and prevents subtle bugs.
takeaways: Audit and rewrite prompt templates to include explicit requirements
Create a project-level prompt file for shared context (style, testing, architecture)
Run a validation suite after each template change to catch regressions early
